Turn practical troubleshooting expertise into smarter AI.
Contribute your field service knowledge to a technical project helping next-generation AI systems learn, reason, and perform through real-world input.
📍 Role details
• 🌐 Global | Fully remote
• Contract type: Contractor
• Compensation: $60–$110 per hour
• Payment terms: Not specified
• Openings: 20
💡 The opportunity
• Apply extensive equipment diagnostics experience to support AI model training.
• No prior AI experience required—your technical domain knowledge is what matters.

• Interpret electrical schematics and hydraulic and pneumatic diagrams to assess equipment function.
• Diagnose equipment faults and performance issues using technical documentation.
• Analyze PLC logic and industrial controls, identifying root causes and recommending evidence-based solutions.
• Document troubleshooting approaches, findings, and corrective actions in clear reports.
• Evaluate relevant NFPA 70/79, ASME A17.1, and OSHA requirements.
• Share practical maintenance, service, and repair insights with diverse audiences.
🎯 What you’ll bring
• Preferred: 8+ years troubleshooting industrial, HVAC, elevator, hydraulic, heavy vehicle, marine, rail, utility, or telecom equipment.
• Advanced proficiency interpreting wiring diagrams, schematics, and fluid-power layouts.
• Deep familiarity with PLC programming, industrial controls, and fault-finding processes.
• Strong knowledge of US safety and operational codes.
• Exceptional written and verbal communication; technical service report experience is a plus.
Help turn years of field experience into valuable AI training knowledge.

If you're buying AI for your clinic the way you bought your PMS, it will fail. 

Why? The SOCIAL contract between clinics and their tech suppliers has changed. The LEGAL contract hasn't.

We learned this the hard way, and recently lost a client. 

At Coherent, we deploy and manage AI across patient admin and operations. New enquiries. Intake. Booking. Payment. Support. Engagement. Retention. Everything you need to serve patients that isn't clinical...

The promise sounds simple: engage every patient without hiring more staff.

Delivering on it isn't. 

It's not pay money, get solution. 

It's a 24/7 job of managing context, governing procedures, and adapting workflows as the real world pressure-tests them.

When a clinic launches a new service line, the answer isn't "add it to the drop-down menu." It is to account for the 1000 ways the service line might show up in a patient interaction, and to design for all of them. 

The old contract:
→ Pay money, get tech
→ One-way: buyer assesses, supplier delivers
→ Procurement process

The new contract:
→ Feedback, spotting issues, fixing them together
→ Two-way: both sides assessing, both sides building
→ Partnership with a shared understanding of what 100% vs 99.9% vs 99% success looks

Healthcare buyers and suppliers should be ASSESSING EACH OTHER.

Deployment, culture change, governance - you only get through them if both sides can work together.

We got it wrong; we didn't spend enough time on the "working together" part. We rushed implementation to hit exec's timelines - not what we know to be best practice. 

It felt great to go live, and then kicked us in the back 5 months later when we struggled to get buy in with the team on the ground.

That's on us. But it was also a reminder of what an AI-ready healthcare provider looks like.

The ones I think will emerge as tech-first market leaders look at the full picture - internal and external. 

It is easy to point the finger at the third party and say "it was you." 

Much harder to point the finger internally, and say "that's on us - let's work together to fix it." 

That tension didn't exist with old-world SaaS procurement. The accountability lines were clearer. 

But now, if you "procure AI" you'll end up with a supplier that fails.  

Much better to partner with your supplier so that you get results.

TCS, Infosys, HCLTech, Wipro and Tech Mahindra together shed 7,389 employees in FY26. A year earlier they added 12,718. TCS alone cut about 23,460, ending at 584,519, one of the biggest single-year workforce reductions by any Indian company. Through the first nine months of FY26, the big players' combined net hiring was just 17 people. Infosys, the relative outlier, grew by 5,016 to 328,594, then slipped by 532 in Q1 FY27.

This isn't a slowdown. It's a repricing.
Wipro says AI freed up the capacity of roughly 20,000 employees. Clients have noticed. At TCS, about 80% of business-services contracts are now tied to outcomes, double the share before generative AI. Clients no longer pay for bodies, they pay for results. That is a very different business.

Who's squeezed?
The pyramid is turning into a diamond. Firms are trimming mid and senior grades, while Wipro cut its fresher hiring guidance to 7,500-8,000. Entry-level work like testing, support and routine coding is exactly what AI does well.

The paradox: TCS says over 270,000 of its people now hold advanced AI/ML skills, and deals are still flowing. Demand for technology services isn't disappearing. Demand for undifferentiated headcount is.

What to do about it:
- Individuals: Move from "doing the task" to "owning the outcome". Learn to orchestrate AI, not compete with it.
- Leaders: Stop measuring scale by headcount. Revenue per employee is the new scoreboard.
- Freshers: Build real projects and show judgment. Certificates alone won't stand out.

The industry isn't dying. It's shedding its old skin. The only question is whether you're shedding with it or being shed.

Bring the Factory, Not Just the Sales Office

There is a recipe every fast-growing tech economy has followed, and it has nothing to do with tax breaks. China, Japan, South Korea did not get rich importing foreign products — they got rich insisting foreign companies build, hire, and teach locally, for years.

China proved it works: 1994–2022, foreign automakers could only sell in China through joint ventures capped at 50% ownership. Research found 27% of workers who left a JV moved straight to a domestic automaker, carrying real knowledge with them.

The AI era is running the same playbook, faster:

 👉 AWS committed to training 100,000 Saudi citizens in cloud and AI as part of its HUMAIN deal
👉 NVIDIA and HUMAIN launched upskilling in AI and robotics for thousands of Saudi developers
👉 Huawei committed to a 5-year center training 25,000 people in AI, cloud, and big data
None of this is fast. Saudi Arabia’s own labor ministry admits a 50% hiring gap in AI roles. 

Localization done properly is a multi-year commitment, not a press release.

For IT companies: if you’re entering markets building sovereign tech capacity, a license and a sales office won’t be enough. Winning the largest contracts now means arriving with a full package — IP-sharing structure, real local development presence, and training built for the engineers who will co-develop your next version themselves.

Plan for a five-year relationship, not a five-month sales cycle.

Twelve contracts in eight years can read as a brilliant, varied career or as a CV nobody quite knows what to do with, and having sat on both sides of the hiring table, I can tell you the difference is usually in how the story is told. 

I was quoted in The Washington Post this week in Julia Carpenter's piece on telling your career story when you're bouncing from job to job (link in the comments but behind a paywall I am afraid). The question every hiring manager quietly asks of a long-term freelancer is whether they can lead a team and stay the course, so the smart move is to answer it before its asked. 

1. Tell your story your way. If you've had twelve separate roles and leave a recruiter to work out your story for themselves, most wont bother. Group your contracts under one consulting banner, with a line that explains the thread running through them, and you've curated your own narrative and done the hard work for them. 

2. Sell the speed. A permanent hire is usually given 100 days to find their feet, while an interim is expected to be adding value by Wednesday. We recently rebuilt a senior operations leaders CV around what he achieved in his first 90 days in each role, and within weeks he had two transformation interviews. 

3. Invest in training ahead of the market. Nobody is nominating you for their leadership programme, so set aside a personal development budget each year and spend it with your longer-term plan in mind. Keep a close eye on where your sector is heading, whether that's AI reshaping your function, new regulation or a shift in what boards expect, and build those skills before clients start asking for them. The interim HR director who got to grips with AI in workforce planning early is the one getting the calls now, while others are still catching up. 

4. Cultivate advocates. Permanent staff inherit sponsors through the organisation chart, while freelancers have to earn them client by client, and at senior level what counts is who knows you and what they know you for. 

5. Be aspirational about where you're heading. Know your career plan and choose contracts that move you towards it, instead of saying yes to whatever lands in your inbox. An interim finance director with her sights on a CFO role in a private equity-backed business might turn down a long, comfortable contract in favour of a shorter assignment inside a portfolio company, because that single line on her CV changes the conversation with every headhunter in the sector.

Freelancers and interims, what's the hardest part of explaining your career to a hiring manager?

you're hiring someone who cut API response times from 2 seconds to 200 milliseconds.

But a team built from employees, freelancers and AI agents doesn't run itself. Here's where it actually breaks down, most often:

- No one has actually said who makes the final call
- Ownership is split across three employment models and written down nowhere
- The freelancer ships the fix, but no one defined when they're supposed to leave

Result: your best problem-solver spends their energy on alignment meetings instead of the actual problem.

Buying skills instead of titles only works if every project has one clear owner; regardless of whether that person is on payroll, on a three-month contract, or an agent.

What actually holds up in practice: single point of accountability per project, or distributed ownership?

Pay moved as well.

Our median permanent salary increased from £80k in Q1 to around £90k in Q3, with the £80k to £100k band the busiest part of the permanent market for us this year so far. Product carried the highest median salary below leadership at £95k, with AI & Data at around £90k. 

Contract activity strengthened as well, with placements up 150% quarter on quarter, across twice as many clients. Median contractor pay across our book is £500 a day (mainly outside IR35 roles), with Product at £580, AI & Data at £550 and Security at £650. 

Across Pulse, vacancy flow increased 34% from Q1 to Q3, while first interview activity increased 58% over the same period. 

The increase in vacancy flow matters because it has kept pace with our growing team.

The other big theme was conversion.

Our CV-to-interview ratio was just under 2:1, with plenty of searches effectively 1:1. Our vacancy-to-placement ratio is around 2:1 year to date, and 100% with several exclusive clients.

That tells us a tighter brief, deep qualification and commitment to the Pulse process are producing better outcomes.

Dozens of people started new roles through Pulse during Q3, while contractor extensions meant more people continuing in work.

It’s been incredible to see the Pulse Experience in action! Deep discovery and qualification, clear communication and accountability throughout the process are showing up in stronger conversion and better outcomes for our clients.

Our mission stays the same: give everyone we interact with a great experience, regardless of the outcome.

We enter the final stretch of 2026 with plenty of opportunity in front of us.

That stopped being a summer internship a while ago. It's a 10-month audition now.

#Draup just analyzed #Fortune500 job postings and found internships and contract roles now make up 27% of early-career hiring, up from 13% in 2020. And since late 2022, employment for 22 to 25 year olds is down 2.4% while 35 to 40 year olds are up 11.4%.

So the door hasn't closed for freshers. The hallway just got a lot longer.

If I were starting out today, here's how I'd spend those 9.7 months:
→ Pick one boring workflow your team hates and fix it with AI in month one, not month nine
→ Write down the before and after in hours, because a manager can defend a number in a headcount meeting
→ Get good at checking AI output, since mentions of AI Literacy in postings are up 725% in a year
→ Show your work to whoever owns the budget. Your mentor isn't the one signing off
→ Ask about conversion in week two, as a plan rather than a demand

The internship is the interview, treat it like one.

A lot of companies don’t have a hiring problem.

They have a problem-definition problem.

I learnt this during my transition into data.

In 2024, I had a conversation with a Group Director before starting a contract.

He said something I’ll never forget:

“Henry, I don’t really know what to call you. I don’t know what job title to give you. But I know you can fix this problem for us.”

That conversation changed how I think about technical roles.

Because I’ve seen the same thing play out across different projects and organisations.

A business has a problem.

Someone decides they need technology to solve it.

Then HR gets involved.

A job description gets created.

And suddenly the organisation is looking for:

Data Engineering + DevOps + AI + Data Science + Analytics + Cloud Architecture.

All in one role.

Then everyone wonders why the salary expectations are high.

But here’s the question I think should come first:

What problem are we actually hiring this person to solve?

For example:

Your data infrastructure is messy.

Your systems don’t talk to each other properly.

Your business definitions aren’t consistent.

Your pipelines are unreliable.

Your reporting requires manual intervention.

And then the organisation says:

“We need someone to implement AI.”

Maybe.

But perhaps the first problem isn’t AI.

Perhaps it’s the infrastructure underneath it.

Perhaps it’s the data.

Perhaps it’s the processes.

Perhaps nobody has clearly defined what the business actually wants the AI to achieve.

And this is where things get interesting.

Sometimes you can build the quick solution.

The stakeholder needs it ASAP.

You know it will work.

But you also know it won’t scale with the organisation.

So you have a choice:

Build what they need today.

Or build what they will probably need tomorrow.

Neither answer is automatically right.

It depends on the business constraints.

Budget.

Time.

Risk.

Growth.

Technical debt.

Expected value.

The important thing is making the trade-off consciously.

Because I’ve learned that good technical work isn’t always about saying:

“Here’s the technology we should use.”

Sometimes it’s saying:

“Before we choose the technology, let’s make sure we’ve defined the problem correctly.”

And I think the same principle applies to hiring.

Don’t start with:

“We need a Data Engineer.”

Start with:

“What needs to be fixed?”

Then ask:

What capabilities are required to fix it?

Then:

What role should own those capabilities?

Then:

What technology does that person actually need to work with?

That sequence can completely change the job description.

And potentially the person you end up hiring.

Because a job description shouldn’t be a shopping list of technologies.

It should be a description of the problem someone is being trusted to solve.

That’s something I’m paying much more attention to as I continue building my career across data, engineering and AI.

DPA to AIA- ( AI ADDENDUM)
Currently doing this in retrospect to cover all existing vendors with AI exposure(ALMOST ALL)

Your vendor shipped an AI feature last quarter. 
Your contract was signed two years ago. 
Which one governs your data?

Nobody checks. 

That's the gap an AI addendum exists to close.
Most Master Agreements say nothing about training. 
So a vendor can fine-tune on your prompts, route them through a model supplier you never approved, and call it product improvement. 
Legal, because you never said no.

A real addendum says no, in writing, and in five places.
No training on your data, extended to every subcontractor and model supplier. 
By clause, not by policy.

No retraining, fine-tuning or model swap without your approval. 
A silent model change is a new risk assessment you never got to run.
No change of sub-processor or model supplier without 30 days notice and a right to object.
Residency that covers inference, caches, indexes, backups and remote support access. 
Not just where the database sits.

Incident notice within 48 hours, with "AI Incident" actually defined and suspected incidents included.
Then comes the clause most people skim. 
Meaningful Human Oversight, defined. 
A person who understands the system, can assess the output, and has real authority to override it.

Fail that test and the indemnity shifts to you.
"Human in the loop" is not just a safeguard.
 It's a liability clause.

Before you sign, ask one thing. 
Can your reviewer actually say no?

Guess which occupation took the biggest hit to junior hiring in this study. Not tech. Legal.

New 41-country study, 22 occupation groups. Legal down 4.9 points on junior share, worse than computer and mathematical roles, finance, sales, management.

That's most of Malta's professional services economy in one list. Every one of those trades runs on apprenticeship, learn the craft doing junior work under someone senior. Memos, reconciliations, due diligence, contract review. Exactly what AI already does fine, and exactly what juniors have always used to learn the job.

Doesn't mean keep AI off those tasks. Just means figuring out what juniors do instead, so they still learn something.

Source note: "How Does AI Change Labor Demand? Evidence from 41 Countries," Chandar & Klein Teeselink, Sept 2026.

Senior QA / Senior Quality Engineer your value is judgment, not execution. 

A Senior QA / Senior Quality Engineer should not simply be a faster version of a QA Engineer.

That is one of the biggest misconceptions in QA career progression.

Being senior does not mean:
Writing more test cases.
Finding more defects.
Automating more scenarios.
Executing regression faster.
Knowing more tools.

Those things can demonstrate experience.
But they are not what makes someone senior.
The real shift is judgment.

A Senior QA should be able to look at a change and ask:
What is the real risk here?
Which customer journeys could be affected?
Where should we test this?

What belongs at unit, integration, API, contract, backend acceptance, or E2E level?
What should be automated?
What is not worth automating?
Which edge cases actually matter?
What evidence do we need before release?
What can we consciously leave untested?
That last question is important.

Seniority is not about trying to test everything.
It is about knowing what deserves the most attention.
A Senior QA should also start seeing patterns that others may miss.
Repeated production defects.
Fragile integrations.
Weak testability.
Missing lower-layer coverage.
Unstable automation.

Poor test data.
Risky architecture decisions.
Gaps in observability.
Patterns across releases.
And then do something with that insight.
Not just report the problem.
Influence how the team solves it.
That means the role also changes from individual execution toward enabling others.
Mentor junior engineers.
Review test approaches.
Challenge assumptions.

Help Engineering improve testability.
Support better automation decisions.
Bring risk into Product discussions.
Improve release confidence.
Help the team learn from incidents.
A strong Senior QA should make the whole team better.
Not become the person who must personally test every difficult feature.
There is another important change at this level.

You start moving from:
“Here is what I tested.”
to:
“Here is what I believe the risk is, here is the evidence, and here is my recommendation.”
That is a very different level of contribution.
Technical depth still matters.

(Long post alert: this topic can't be covered briefly!) What would an AI-native law firm in India look like? 

Disruptivity Times, a speculative news site, recently imagined one version in a headline dated 2031: DLA Piper ends the billable hour for corporate work. Clients move to flat subscriptions, AI does the first pass on every contract, and a named partner owns the final advice. Its fiction, for now. But it raises some interesting questions. 

A real version has already started. Global banks are telling their law firms that if AI cuts the work, it should cut the bill. That pressure will reach Indian firms through the same clients. And when it does, buying more software won't be the answer. 

Most Indian firms can now say they use AI. Far fewer can say what it has earned them. 

Whether the invoice is hourly, fixed or per appearance, most quotes are built from time and headcount. Make a junior 40% faster and you either quote less or carry idle capacity. When pricing tracks effort, efficiency is a cost, not a return. In India, the case for AI here rests less on cutting labour costs than on doing work that was never affordable before.

An AI-native firm in India would be built differently: 

1) Lawyers who work with AI, build with it, and own the workflows, wherever the technology comes from; 

2) Workflows where machines handle routine production, from first drafts to research and chronologies, and lawyers review, negotiate, argue and sign off; 

3) An AI first pass to scope matters, whether a data room or a case record, before the fee is agreed; 

4) Routine work priced by output or stage, and judgement priced on what it's worth; and 

5) Verification and data confidentiality discipline treated as the product, not a compliance step. 

What changes is where the lawyers time goes, and what the firm is paid for. 

It would also reach clients no effort-priced firm can. Over six crore registered small businesses sign contracts no lawyer has read, many in regional languages, because a lawyers day costs more than the contract is worth. A firm that can price that work low and still profit at volume isn't just growing its margin. Its widening access to legal help. 

Those unread contracts are also where many disputes begin, and Indian courts already carry over 5.6 crore pending cases. Disputes teams working through that volume need the same rebuild: research, chronologies and first drafts handled by machines, so lawyers can spend their time on strategy and the courtroom.

Becoming AI-native doesn't have to wait for ownership reform. Fixed and capped fees have always been permitted, and nothing stops a firm hiring engineers or working with technology providers. 

At NYAI, that's the tech infrastructure we provide and build with firms, whether they're starting AI-native or rebuilding to get there. 

Capable lawyers make a firm AI-native. The right pricing makes it pay.

Hiring a technology leader? Secured new investment? Announced a transformation strategy?

How quickly will that ambition become measurable business value?

If you need someone who understands technology, business, process and the numbers, and can take ownership of delivery, I can help.

I’m immediately available for interim, contract or permanent roles.

Whether you have an open vacancy, funding for growth, an acquisition to integrate or a strategy that needs turning into action, this is the work I enjoy.

My approach connects four things:

1. BUSINESS STRATEGY
    Agree the outcomes: growth, margin, customer experience, efficiency and resilience.
2. CAPABILITY HEAT MAP
    Show where the business is strong, where gaps are holding it back and which changes deserve investment first.
3. IT STRATEGY
    Translate those priorities into technology choices, a credible business case and a funded roadmap.
4. TECHNOLOGY DELIVERY
    Deliver in manageable releases, with clear owners, adoption plans and benefits measured against the starting point.

For example: profitable ecommerce growth might require better customer insight and fewer manual order handoffs. The roadmap then connects data, commerce and fulfilment, strengthens cyber controls and applies automation or AI where it adds value.

This covers Data, Cyber, Ecommerce, Process and AI, supported by cloud, integration and core business systems.

I structure delivery around “value drops”: usable improvements that start generating benefits while the wider transformation progresses.

My aim is measurable ROI within 6–12 months of the relevant investment, where the business case supports it. Each drop needs a clear cost, accountable owner and a benefit we can evidence.

A multi-year strategy should not mean a multi-year wait for every benefit.

Results I’ve helped deliver include 50% lower on-premise data-centre costs, £1.5m annual payment-fee savings and software releases moving from weekly to daily.

Have a vacancy, investment plan or transformation challenge where this combination would help? Message me. Introductions to people hiring or leading change are very welcome.

What would your business want its first value drop to achieve?
